design_detail: Systematic review without meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD42024565395; PRISMA 2020 and SWiM reporting) of original studies of antipsychotic treatment for amphetamine-induced psychosis (AIP: dexamphetamine, levamphetamine, lisdexamfetamine or methamphetamine) and cannabis-induced psychosis, asking which regimen (drug, dose, duration, mode) best relieves symptoms and which has the lowest relapse rate after treatment stops. Nine databases and trial registries were searched from inception to 25 March 2026, plus Google Scholar and citation chasing, without language or date limits. Fifteen studies: 11 on AIP (8 randomized trials with 514 participants, 1 quasi-experimental study, 1 prospective and 1 retrospective cohort; 724 participants in all) and 4 on cannabis-induced psychosis (1872). Narrative synthesis grouped by treatment duration and design; the authors computed within-group standardized mean differences (baseline against end of treatment) and odds ratios where the data allowed. Risk of bias with RoB 2 for randomized trials and JBI tools for the other designs. Read: the full article on the publisher's site (OnlineFirst, open access), including Tables 1 to 4 (rendered as text), the conflict-of-interest and funding statements, author affiliations and the reference list; Figures 1 to 3 (PRISMA flowchart, risk-of-bias traffic-light and bar plots) are images and were not read for values; Supplemental Material A to E (a Word file) was not read.
can_establish: Which studies of antipsychotics in amphetamine-induced psychosis, randomized or not, had been published by March 2026, what each reported on symptoms, tolerability, service use and substance use, and that none followed participants after the antipsychotic was stopped.
cannot_establish: Whether antipsychotics relieve amphetamine-induced psychosis more than abstinence and time do (the review's effect sizes are changes from baseline within each arm, and only two small placebo-controlled trials compare a drug with no drug: one in people stabilised before discharge, the other in people whose symptoms had largely subsided by the network meta-analysis's account), which drug or dose is best (no pooled comparison), or how long to treat (no data after treatment stops).

sample.recruitment: Medline (Ovid), CINAHL Complete, APA PsycInfo, Embase, CENTRAL, the WHO ICTRP, ClinicalTrials.gov, Web of Science Core Collection and Scopus from inception to 25 March 2026, with a strategy developed with a hospital librarian; Google Scholar (first 200 records by rank); backward and forward citation chasing of the included articles (Methods › Information sources and search strategy). The AIP studies came from China and the USA (3 each) and Iran, Malaysia and Thailand (2 each), in inpatient (psychiatric and rehabilitation) and outpatient settings (Results › Amphetamine-induced psychosis studies, 1st paragraph). Editors' sums of the AIP study sizes in Table 1 give the 724 of the abstract; the trial sizes give 514.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: peer-reviewed original empirical studies of the post-acute management (persisting beyond intoxication) of AIP or cannabis-induced psychosis meeting DSM-5-TR or ICD-11 criteria or their legacy equivalents, any age; randomized, uncontrolled and non-randomized trials and observational studies; any antipsychotic, against another antipsychotic, placebo or no treatment. Excluded: other substituted amphetamines (such as MDMA) and non-amphetamine stimulants (such as cocaine), psychosis occurring only during intoxication or withdrawal, studies of people with earlier primary psychotic disorders, Parkinson's disease or dementia, and reviews, opinion pieces, letters, editorials, protocols, qualitative studies, conference abstracts and case reports or series (Methods › Eligibility criteria). Full criteria are in Supplemental Material B (not read).
sample.demographics: Mostly adult men aged 18 to 65 (Results › Study characteristics, 1st paragraph). AIP randomized trials: mean ages 22.7 to 40.0 years and 70.5% to 100% men; diagnoses described as methamphetamine psychosis or methamphetamine dependence with psychosis in five trials and in amphetamine terms in three (amphetamine-induced psychotic disorder, Farnia 2014; amphetamine dependence, with methamphetamine use and psychotic symptoms as the threshold, Sulaiman 2013; amphetamine psychosis, Leelahanaj 2005) (Table 1).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; trial-level early discontinuation, retention and loss to follow-up are tabulated (Table 3), for example 28% against 55% lost to follow-up on paliperidone and placebo in one trial.
sample.selection_effects: The review is restricted to peer-reviewed literature, but one AIP study (Sulaiman 2011, a prospective cohort) is a doctoral dissertation. Two of the eight AIP trials are placebo-controlled; the other six compare antipsychotics. Most trials are small single-site inpatient studies in Asia, and studies of people with earlier primary psychoses were excluded. The list of excluded full texts is not in the article, so omissions cannot be checked.

exposure.measurement: Not an exposure study; the intervention is antipsychotic treatment, oral in all AIP trials. The review expresses doses as a percentage of the British National Formulary maximum daily dose (Methods › Data synthesis, 1st paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions in the AIP trials: 10% to 100% of the BNF maximum across trials; 25 to 28 days in five trials, 6 weeks in one (Farnia 2014), 8 weeks in one (Sulaiman 2013) and 12 weeks in one (Wang 2019) (Results › Amphetamine-induced psychosis studies, 2nd paragraph; Table 1). Non-randomized studies: as-needed olanzapine take-home packs (Coffin 2024), 14 days of aripiprazole (Sulaiman 2011) and unspecified antipsychotics during admission (Herbst 2022) (Table 1).
exposure.polysubstance: Table 1 gives 'Other substance use' as No for all eight AIP trials and for Sulaiman 2011, Not specified for Coffin 2024 and Yes for Herbst 2022, without defining the entry; comorbid substance use (excluding nicotine) was an exclusion criterion in 5 of the 15 studies (Results › Study characteristics, 1st paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not reported by the review. The discussion notes that the share of recovery due to antipsychotics, as against natural recovery after a crisis and the effect of abstinence, could not be determined from the data (Discussion, 5th paragraph).

comparison.controls: AIP randomized trials: another antipsychotic in six and placebo in two (Sulaiman 2013, aripiprazole; Wang 2019, paliperidone extended-release); non-randomized studies: no comparator (Coffin 2024, Sulaiman 2011) or people not treated with antipsychotics (Herbst 2022) (Table 1).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not reported per study; earlier primary psychotic disorders were an exclusion criterion of the review.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: As for polysubstance use: not defined per study.

outcomes.instruments: Primary: psychotic symptoms on validated scales (PANSS, BPRS, SAPS, SANS, CGI-S). Secondary: tolerability and side effects (Simpson–Angus Scale, Barnes Akathisia Rating Scale, AIMS, adverse events, retention), amphetamine- or cannabis-related service use, ongoing use (craving scales, urine drug screens) and social outcomes (Methods › Eligibility criteria › Outcome).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard rating scales; the review does not discuss the floors of the PANSS or BPRS when interpreting low baseline scores.
outcomes.operationalization: Within-group Cohen's d computed as (baseline mean minus end-point mean) divided by the pooled SD of baseline and end point, interpreted with Sawilowsky's labels from very small to huge; odds ratios for binary outcomes; between-group p values as reported by the trials (Methods › Measures of effect; Tables 2 and 3).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; narrative synthesis of one primary outcome focus (symptom reduction), the relapse question and four secondary outcome groups (tolerability, service use, substance use, social outcomes), reported study by study.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable at review level. Two reviewers independently screened titles, abstracts and full texts, with a third for unresolved disagreements; two independently extracted data; two independently appraised each study (Methods › Selection process; Data collection process; Risk of bias assessment and quality appraisal).

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooled estimate: a biostatistician advised that meta-analysis was inappropriate because of heterogeneity, few placebo controls and too few direct comparisons for a network meta-analysis (Methods › Data synthesis). Within-group SMDs for AIP, baseline to end (Table 2): aripiprazole over 14 days in the cohort d = 1.942 (1.462 to 2.423); every arm of the five 4-week trials d = 3.402 to 5.495 (Wang 2020, Verachai 2014, Wang 2016, Samiei 2016, Leelahanaj 2005), with between-group p = 0.06, 0.32, 0.73, not significant and 0.07. Farnia 2014: between-group p < 0.001 on SAPS and 0.08 on SANS, SMDs not calculable. Placebo-controlled trials: Sulaiman 2013, between-group p = 0.032 (MMRM, favouring aripiprazole); Wang 2019, PANSS 37.8 (SD 5.4) to 34 (3.9) on paliperidone and 36.2 (4.3) to 32.9 (1.9) on placebo, between-group p = 0.006 (reported from Cox regression). Tolerability (Table 3): extrapyramidal symptoms in 15 of 29 (51.72%) on haloperidol vs 0 of 29 on olanzapine, OR 63.07 (3.52 to 1129.74), p = 0.0049, and early discontinuation 10 (34%) vs 2 (7%), OR 7.12 (1.4 to 36.18), p = 0.0182 (Leelahanaj 2005); discontinuation for adverse events 7 of 21 (33%) on aripiprazole vs 0 of 21 on risperidone, OR 22.24 (1.18 to 420.39), p = 0.0386, retention 19.9 vs 24 days, p = 0.007 (Wang 2016); Simpson–Angus scores 0.1 to 1.8 on paliperidone vs 0.1 to 3.1 on risperidone, between-group p < 0.01 (Wang 2020); lost to follow-up 11 (28%) on paliperidone vs 22 (55%) on placebo, OR 0.31 (0.12 to 0.79), p = 0.0139 (Wang 2019). Service use: psychiatric readmission within 90 days 11 of 35 (31.4%) treated vs 4 of 34 (11.8%) untreated, OR printed as 1.29 (0.63 to 2.63), p = 0.4893 (Herbst 2022); drug-related emergency visits IRR 0.96 (0.9 to 1.03) in the 12 months after as-needed olanzapine packs (Coffin 2024). Editors' check: the within-group d values reproduce from the printed means and SDs except as noted in reporting issues 1 and 10.
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42024565395, stated to be prospectively registered (Methods, 1st paragraph); the registered protocol was not compared with the review, and the article reports no deviations.
analysis.selective_reporting: Adverse-event categories in which no study found a significant difference between comparators were left out of Tables 3 and 4 and are only listed by name (Table 3, footnote c), so tolerability is shown selectively. Per-study risk-of-bias judgments are given only in Figures 2 and 3 (images) and Supplemental Material D.
analysis.power: Not addressed; the AIP trials had 37 to 120 participants (Table 1).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Eight small, short AIP trials, six of them head-to-head: symptoms fell markedly within every arm, and the head-to-head trials mostly found no significant difference between drugs; in two placebo-controlled trials, one enrolling people stabilised before discharge (baseline PANSS about 37) and one whose baseline the review does not give, the antipsychotic did better on the PANSS (p = 0.032 and 0.006). Haloperidol caused far more extrapyramidal symptoms than olanzapine in one trial, and aripiprazole more discontinuation for adverse events than risperidone in another. No study followed participants after the antipsychotic was stopped.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that the review "found support for the effectiveness of antipsychotic drugs" in reducing symptoms (Abstract › Conclusions). Gaps: (1) that support rests mainly on changes from baseline within each arm, which the review computes and labels huge (d = 3.4 to 5.5) but which cannot separate a drug effect from recovery with abstinence and time; the discussion concedes this (Discussion, 5th paragraph) and the Conclusion section is more cautious (antipsychotics may be efficacious; a clear conclusion cannot be drawn), but the abstract is not; (2) two of the huge effect sizes (Samiei 2016) were computed with an end-point SD of zero; (3) the discussion's statement that antipsychotics carry a markedly worse side-effect burden than placebo or non-antipsychotic drugs is not backed by any comparison shown in the review; (4) the abstract's no-regimen-was-superior fits the head-to-head trials taken together, but Table 2 reports a significant between-group difference on positive symptoms in one of them (Farnia 2014), which the review describes in conflicting ways (reporting issue 2).

timeline.event: Systematic review of six randomized trials of antipsychotics in amphetamine psychosis; all six are among this review's eight AIP trials
Meta-analysis of transition from substance-induced psychoses to schizophrenia, cited in this review's introduction for an amphetamine figure of 22% (with a misprinted interval; reporting issue 7)

Network meta-analysis of six head-to-head trials in methamphetamine psychosis, all six among this review's AIP trials; this review notes that it needed statistical assumptions because of missing data from two trials
Scoping review of substance-specific treatment responses in induced psychoses (Ricci et al.), described in this review's introduction as limited by its broad focus.
This review: 15 studies, searches to 25 March 2026; no study with follow-up after antipsychotics were stopped.
24-month randomized trial of aripiprazole or paliperidone against usual care in stimulant-induced psychosis, published after this review's search

replication.where_it_stands: The most complete inventory of studies of antipsychotics in amphetamine-induced psychosis to March 2026, and the first review read here to establish that no study has followed people after treatment stops. All its AIP trials are shared with the earlier reviews, so agreement with them is not independent replication; the three reviews disagree on some trial-level facts (results and risk of bias of individual trials). A trial against usual care (Chung et al., 2026) appeared after its search.

funding.funder: None: the authors state that they received no financial support for the research, authorship or publication (Funding).
funding.declared_conflicts: M.D. has received speaker's honoraria from Camurus, Indivior and Lundbeck Australia and expenses from RANZCP in the past 5 years, and was an investigator on a Pfizer-funded varenicline trial more than 10 years ago; S.P. holds a Metro North Clinician Research Fellowship (2024 to 2027) and has received honoraria in the past 5 years from CSL Seqirus, Lundbeck/Otsuka, Johnson & Johnson, RANZCP, Queensland Psychotherapy Training and Tasmania Health; the employers of J.G.S. (University of Queensland and QIMR Berghofer Medical Research Institute) have received research funds from Janssen-Cilag, Otsuka and Lundbeck in return for his lectures and advisory-board participation; the other four authors declare none (Declaration of conflicting interests).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from The University of Queensland (School of Medicine, School of Psychology, Child Health Research Centre), Metro North Mental Health (Metro North Hospital and Health Service), The Prince Charles Hospital (including its Library Services) and Children's Health Queensland, Brisbane. Two authors have received honoraria from, or have employers funded by, manufacturers of antipsychotics (Lundbeck/Otsuka, Janssen-Cilag, Johnson & Johnson); recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized discontinuation trial in people who have recovered from methamphetamine psychosis on an antipsychotic, comparing continuation with tapering to placebo over at least 6 to 12 months with relapse as the primary outcome and urine-verified use recorded; and, for the acute episode, a placebo-controlled trial on top of supervised abstinence.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (AIP and cannabis-induced psychosis by DSM-5-TR or ICD-11 criteria or legacy equivalents), intervention (antipsychotics), comparators (another antipsychotic, placebo or no treatment), outcomes and two research questions are stated (Objectives and research questions; Methods › Eligibility criteria).
Prospectively registered on PROSPERO (CRD42024565395); the registered protocol was not compared with the review here, and the article reports no deviations or justification for any.

Randomized trials, uncontrolled and non-randomized trials and observational studies were all permitted without an explanation of the choice; the relapse question would justify observational designs, but no reason is given.

Nine databases and registries with a librarian-built strategy (Supplemental Material C), Google Scholar, backward and forward citation chasing, no language or date limits, and a search about 6 months before online publication. But eligibility is restricted to peer-reviewed literature without a stated reason (Methods › Eligibility criteria › Study design/characteristics), and the restriction is not kept (a dissertation is included). AMSTAR 2 gives 'partial yes' only when publication restrictions are justified, so, applied as written, the item is not met; no consultation of content experts is reported either.
Two independent reviewers screened titles, abstracts and full texts, with a third for unresolved disagreements (Methods › Selection process).
Two team members independently extracted the data and resolved disagreements together (Methods › Data collection process).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: No list of the full texts excluded, with reasons, appears in the article; the PRISMA flowchart is an image, and the supplements the article names (A, search checklist; B, eligibility table; C, search terms; D, appraisal of non-randomized studies; E, secondary outcomes) do not include one.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives location, data period, setting, sponsorship, numbers per arm, diagnosis and severity threshold, age and sex, other substance use, interventions and comparators with doses (also as a share of the BNF maximum), duration and outcomes.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: RoB 2 for the randomized trials, by two independent assessors, summarized in the text with domain-level plots as images; this covers what AMSTAR 2 requires for trials. The non-randomized studies were appraised with JBI tools collapsed into poor, fair or good ratings, without showing that confounding and selection were assessed.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Sponsorship of each study is given in Table 1 (government, industry, none declared or not listed); one study was industry-sponsored.
No meta-analysis; the decision is explained (Methods › Data synthesis).

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Studies are grouped and ordered by risk of bias, each result is reported with its study's rating, and the Conclusion declines a clear conclusion because of the quality of the data; the discussion notes that natural recovery and abstinence could not be separated from treatment effects. The abstract's conclusion is less cautious (interpretation gap).

Differences in design, population, dose and comparator are described and given as the reason for not pooling; studies are grouped by duration and design, and dose differences between arms are discussed (for example Farnia 2014).

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding (none) and each author's potential conflicts are declared.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Two critical items are not met (4: eligibility restricted to peer-reviewed literature without a stated reason, with AMSTAR 2 applied as written; 7: no list of excluded studies with reasons) and two are only partly met (2 and 9), which gives critically low confidence; read leniently on item 4 (only language limits need a reason), the one remaining critical flaw would give low confidence. The review is otherwise careful (registered, duplicate selection and extraction, RoB 2, a broad search to March 2026 without language or date limits). It may be cited for its inventory of studies, for the absence of any study with follow-up after antipsychotics are stopped, and for the trial-level tolerability and placebo-controlled results it tabulates. Its within-group effect sizes should not be cited as treatment effects, and two of them (Samiei 2016) are computational artefacts.

key_findings.finding: Registered (PROSPERO CRD42024565395) review following PRISMA 2020 and SWiM; nine databases and registries searched from inception to 25 March 2026 without language or date limits, plus Google Scholar (first 200 records) and backward and forward citation chasing; duplicate independent screening, extraction and appraisal; RoB 2 for randomized trials and JBI tools for other designs; meta-analysis judged inappropriate.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 1st paragraph; Methods › Information sources and search strategy; Selection process; Data collection process; Risk of bias assessment and quality appraisal; Data synthesis, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Fifteen studies: 11 on amphetamine-induced psychosis (724 participants) and 4 on cannabis-induced psychosis (1872). The AIP studies are 8 randomized trials with 514 participants (paliperidone extended-release 60 vs risperidone 60, Wang 2020; paliperidone 40 vs placebo 40, Wang 2019; aripiprazole 27 vs risperidone 26, Farnia 2014; haloperidol 44 vs quetiapine 36, Verachai 2014; aripiprazole 19 vs placebo 18, Sulaiman 2013; aripiprazole 21 vs risperidone 21, Wang 2016; haloperidol 22 vs risperidone 22, Samiei 2016; olanzapine 29 vs haloperidol 29, Leelahanaj 2005), a quasi-experimental study (Coffin 2024, 92), a prospective cohort (Sulaiman 2011, 49) and a retrospective cohort (Herbst 2022, 69). Only two trials were placebo-controlled; five lasted 25 to 28 days, the others 6, 8 and 12 weeks.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results; Results › Study characteristics, 1st paragraph; Results › Amphetamine-induced psychosis studies, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 1
key_findings.note: Editors' sums from Table 1 reproduce 724 and 514. The six head-to-head trials are the six of the 2021 network meta-analysis; the two placebo-controlled trials are additional.

key_findings.finding: Risk of bias (RoB 2): five of the eight AIP trials at low risk (Farnia 2014, Sulaiman 2013, Verachai 2014, Wang 2019, Wang 2020); Wang 2016 with some concerns because of dropout (12 of 42); Leelahanaj 2005 and Samiei 2016 at high risk because blinding procedures were not specified. Of the non-randomized AIP studies, Coffin 2024 and Sulaiman 2011 were rated fair and Herbst 2022 poor.
key_findings.note: The 2021 network meta-analysis judged Samiei 2016 and Wang 2016 open-label and at high risk in two domains (study card sc_srisurapanont_2021), and Leelahanaj 2005 is titled as double-blind; the reviews' trial-level judgments differ.

key_findings.finding: Effect sizes are within-group changes, (baseline mean minus end-point mean) divided by the pooled SD, labelled with Sawilowsky's categories. In the five 4-week trials every arm improved (d = 3.402 to 5.495, within-group p < 0.05 or smaller), and none reported a significant between-group difference (p = 0.06 Wang 2020, 0.32 Verachai 2014, 0.73 Wang 2016, not significant Samiei 2016, 0.07 Leelahanaj 2005). In the 14-day aripiprazole cohort the PANSS fell from 79.2 (SD 13.7) to 51.6 (14.7), d = 1.942.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Measures of effect; Results › Primary outcomes › Psychotic symptom reduction › Amphetamine-induced psychosis, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Farnia 2014 (aripiprazole at 50% vs risperidone at 25% of the BNF maximum, 6 weeks): Table 2 gives a between-group p < 0.001 on positive symptoms (SAPS) and 0.08 on negative symptoms (SANS); the text reports favourable reductions in positive but not negative symptoms in the aripiprazole group, and notes that the unequal relative doses limit conclusions.
key_findings.locator: Results › Primary outcomes › Psychotic symptom reduction › Amphetamine-induced psychosis, 3rd paragraph; Table 2, Farnia row
key_findings.note: Table 2's end-point figures for this trial are footnoted as mean changes from baseline (SAPS 10.8 on aripiprazole vs 16.2 on risperidone), which would favour risperidone; the discussion describes the trial differently again (reporting issue 2).

key_findings.finding: Placebo-controlled trials: aripiprazole for 8 weeks in 37 outpatients (Sulaiman 2013) reduced PANSS scores more than placebo (MMRM, between-group p = 0.032; the trial reports improvement on aripiprazole and deterioration on placebo without test statistics), with longer retention (48.74 vs 43.08 days, p = 0.023). Paliperidone extended-release for 84 days in 80 people stabilised in voluntary drug-treatment wards before discharge (Wang 2019; baseline PANSS 37.8 and 36.2) favoured paliperidone (group-by-time interaction from Cox regression, p = 0.006), with fewer lost to follow-up (11, 28%, vs 22, 55%; OR 0.31, 0.12 to 0.79).
key_findings.locator: Results › Primary outcomes › Psychotic symptom reduction › Amphetamine-induced psychosis, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Table 2, Sulaiman 2013 and Wang 2019 rows and footnotes c and d; Table 3, section 2a-2
key_findings.note: This review shows a low symptom level only for Wang 2019 (baseline PANSS 37.8 and 36.2); for Sulaiman 2013 it gives no baseline and its Table 1 threshold is the presence of psychotic symptoms, and the low level comes from the network meta-analysis, which excluded that trial because its participants had recovered from psychotic symptoms (entry PANSS 51.6; study card sc_srisurapanont_2021). The printed Wang 2019 means fall by similar amounts in both arms (3.8 vs 3.3 points; editors' arithmetic), so the reported advantage cannot be seen in them (reporting issue 3).

key_findings.finding: No included study followed participants after antipsychotic treatment was stopped, so the review could not answer which regimen has the lowest relapse rate after cessation, or the optimal duration of treatment, for amphetamine-induced psychosis.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, note; Abstract › Results; Discussion, 3rd and 5th paragraphs; Conclusion

key_findings.finding: Tolerability: all antipsychotic arms showed increased extrapyramidal side effects except the olanzapine arm of one trial and the aripiprazole cohort. Leelahanaj 2005: extrapyramidal symptoms in 15 of 29 (51.72%) on haloperidol vs none on olanzapine (OR 63.07, 3.52 to 1129.74; p = 0.0049) and early discontinuation 10 (34%) vs 2 (7%) (OR 7.12, 1.4 to 36.18; p = 0.0182). Wang 2016: discontinuation because of adverse events 7 of 21 (33%) on aripiprazole vs none on risperidone (OR 22.24, 1.18 to 420.39; p = 0.0386), retention 19.9 vs 24 days (p = 0.007). Wang 2020: Simpson–Angus scores rose less on paliperidone than on risperidone (to 1.8 vs 3.1; p < 0.01). No antipsychotic showed tolerability advantages sufficient, in the authors' view, to prefer it.
key_findings.locator: Results › Secondary outcomes › Tolerability › Global extrapyramidal side effects, 1st paragraph; Attrition, non-adherence and medication refusal, 1st paragraph; Table 3, sections 2a-1 and 2a-2; Discussion, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Table 3 (2a-1) also gives Wang 2016 a between-group p = 0.01 on the Simpson–Angus Scale (aripiprazole 0.1 to 3.4, risperidone 0.2 to 3), where the 2019 review reports no significant difference between the drugs on that scale (study card sc_fluyau_2019); the reviews disagree on this trial's side effects.

key_findings.finding: Non-randomized studies: in a poor-quality retrospective cohort (Herbst 2022), inpatients treated with antipsychotics had a longer initial stay and were readmitted within 90 days in 11 of 35 (31.4%) cases against 4 of 34 (11.8%) untreated (OR printed as 1.29, 0.63 to 2.63; p = 0.4893), with no stratification by severity; after as-needed olanzapine take-home packs, drug-related emergency visits did not change (IRR 0.96, 0.9 to 1.03; p = 0.3; Coffin 2024).
key_findings.locator: Results › Methodological quality, 4th paragraph; Results › Secondary outcomes › Service use, 1st paragraph; Table 3, section 2b
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: the printed counts give a crude OR of about 3.4 for readmission, not 1.29 (reporting issue 8).

key_findings.finding: Ongoing use: in the placebo-controlled trials, craving fell more on aripiprazole than on placebo (Brief Substance Craving Scale, between-group p = 0.015, no effect size; Sulaiman 2013) and more on paliperidone than on placebo (between-group p = 0.03; Wang 2019); the d of 0.951 that the text gives for paliperidone is the fall within the paliperidone arm (0.761 within the placebo arm), not a between-group effect. The only randomized trial with an objective measure found no difference in methamphetamine-positive urine between aripiprazole and placebo at the end (52.6% to 42.9% vs 55.6% to 43.8%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Secondary outcomes › Ongoing substance use, 1st paragraph; Table 3, section 2c
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: by the review's formula the printed within-arm d values (0.951 and 0.761) are approached only with a paliperidone baseline SD of 0.8 rather than the printed 0.08 and with end-point numbers of 29 and 18 (40 minus those lost to follow-up), which give 0.949 and 0.761.

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: data were unsuitable for meta-analysis; there were limited data to show how much of the observed recovery was due to antipsychotics rather than natural recovery after a crisis or the duration of abstinence; no AIP study followed participants after antipsychotics were stopped.

reporting_issues.issue: For Samiei 2016 the end-point SAPS is entered as 0 with no SD in both arms, yet within-group d values of 4.488 and 5.495 with intervals are given; these equal the baseline mean divided by the baseline SD over the square root of 2, that is, the review's formula with an end-point SD of zero (editors' recalculation reproduces both values exactly).
reporting_issues.consequence: The two largest effect sizes in the review are artefacts, and the upper end of the reported range for the 4-week trials (d = 3.402 to 5.495) rests on them; without them the range is 3.40 to 4.75.

reporting_issues.issue: Farnia 2014 is described three ways: the Results say aripiprazole gave favourable reductions in positive but not negative symptoms; the Discussion says aripiprazole and risperidone were effective on positive but not negative symptoms; Table 2 gives within-group p < 0.001 for negative symptoms in both arms, and its end-point figures, footnoted as mean changes from baseline, show larger positive-symptom falls on risperidone (16.2 vs 10.8) and larger negative-symptom falls on aripiprazole (11.25 vs 9.35).
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Results › Primary outcomes › Amphetamine-induced psychosis, 3rd paragraph; Discussion, 1st paragraph; Table 2 (Farnia row) and footnote a
reporting_issues.consequence: The direction of this trial's between-drug result is uncertain here, as it is in the 2019 review (study card sc_fluyau_2019); the trial report should be read before any claim states it.

reporting_issues.issue: For Wang 2019 the between-group result for the PANSS (p = 0.006, favouring paliperidone) is attributed to Cox regression of a group-by-time interaction, a method for time-to-event data, while the printed means fall by similar amounts in both arms (3.8 vs 3.3 points) and the placebo end-point mean is the lower; 55% of the placebo arm were lost to follow-up.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Table 2 (Wang 2019 row) and footnote d; Results › Primary outcomes › Amphetamine-induced psychosis, 4th paragraph; Table 3, section 2a-2
reporting_issues.consequence: What was analysed, and in whom, is unclear; the reported advantage of paliperidone cannot be checked from the review.

reporting_issues.issue: Retention in Sulaiman 2013 is given as 48.74 (SD 0.40) against 43.08 (SD 0.50) days with p = 0.023; SDs of half a day are implausible for time in treatment and would make a difference of 5.7 days far more significant than p = 0.023.
reporting_issues.consequence: The dispersion figures are probably misprinted (perhaps standard errors or another statistic); the retention advantage on aripiprazole is uncertain in size.

reporting_issues.issue: The review is restricted to peer-reviewed literature, but Sulaiman (2011) is a doctoral dissertation. It and the 2013 placebo-controlled trial come from the same author and research programme, and the dissertation's 14-day end-point PANSS (51.6) equals the entry PANSS that the 2021 network meta-analysis gives for the 2013 trial (study card sc_srisurapanont_2021).
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Methods › Eligibility criteria › Study design/characteristics; Table 1 and Table 2 (Sulaiman 2011 rows); reference list (Sulaiman AH 2011; Sulaiman et al. 2013)
reporting_issues.consequence: The two studies may share participants (editors' inference: the placebo-controlled trial may have randomized people after an open-label aripiprazole phase); if so, they are not independent and the trial tested continued treatment after a response.

reporting_issues.issue: The introduction cites Murrie et al. (2020) for a transition rate to schizophrenia after amphetamine-induced psychosis of 22% (95% CI 14%–24%); Murrie et al. give 22% (14% to 34%) (study card sc_murrie_2020).
reporting_issues.consequence: Misprinted upper limit; the interval should not be copied from this review.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion of ongoing use attributes the larger reduction in craving on risperidone than on aripiprazole to Wang et al. (2019), a paliperidone–placebo trial; in Table 3 the comparison is Wang et al. (2016). The same paragraph gives paliperidone in Wang 2020 as 27%–75% of the BNF maximum, where Table 1 gives 25%–75%.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Results › Secondary outcomes › Ongoing substance use, 1st paragraph; Table 3, section 2c

reporting_issues.issue: In Herbst 2022, 11 of 35 treated and 4 of 34 untreated inpatients were readmitted within 90 days, which gives a crude odds ratio of about 3.4 (editors' calculation), while the review prints OR 1.29 (0.63 to 2.63) without saying whether it is adjusted.
reporting_issues.consequence: The only comparison with people not given antipsychotics cannot be interpreted from the review; it is in any case confounded by indication.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion states that people treated with antipsychotics had a markedly worse side-effect burden than those given placebo or non-antipsychotic drugs, but no such comparison is shown: adverse-event categories without a significant between-comparator difference were omitted from Tables 3 and 4, and in both placebo-controlled AIP trials retention was better on the antipsychotic.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Table 3, footnote c; Table 3, section 2a-2
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement should not be cited as a finding of the review.

reporting_issues.issue: Minor arithmetic: the within-group d values for Leelahanaj 2005 are exchanged between arms (by the review's formula haloperidol is 4.752 and olanzapine 4.719, printed the other way round), and the risperidone Simpson–Angus d in Wang 2020 is printed as −2.149 (−3.87 to −0.43) where the printed means and SDs give about −2.85 with a much narrower interval for 60 participants (editors' recalculation).
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Table 2 (Leelahanaj row); Table 3, section 2a-1 (Wang 2020 row)
reporting_issues.consequence: None for the conclusions; shows that the computed effect sizes were not checked.

reporting_issues.issue: The paragraph describing the eight AIP randomized trials gives outcome counts out of 10 studies (psychotic symptoms 9 of 10, tolerability 4 of 10, ongoing use 5 of 10).
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Results › Amphetamine-induced psychosis studies, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the denominators fit neither the 8 trials nor the 11 AIP studies.

disagreements.first_pass: Both trials enrolled people with low symptom levels; the printed Wang 2019 means fall by similar amounts in both arms (3.8 vs 3.3 points; editors' arithmetic), so the reported advantage cannot be seen in them (reporting issue 3). … and only two small placebo-controlled trials, in people with low symptom levels, compare a drug with no drug) … in two placebo-controlled trials in people with low symptom levels (one enrolling people stabilised before discharge) the antipsychotic did better on the PANSS (p = 0.032 and 0.006).
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 21: confirmed, with a correction to the note: 'both trials enrolled people with low symptom levels' is right for Wang 2019 (baseline PANSS 37.8 and 36.2) but not from this review for Sulaiman 2013, for which Hall gives no baseline and whose Table 1 threshold is the presence of psychotic symptoms; the low level comes from the network meta-analysis's figure (PANSS 51.6), which the card should cite. The same wording recurs in cannot_establish and results_show.
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed in Table 1 (Sulaiman 2013: severity threshold, methamphetamine use and the presence of psychotic symptoms), Table 2 (Sulaiman 2013 baseline and end values N/A; Wang 2019 PANSS 37.8 and 36.2) and Primary outcomes › Amphetamine-induced psychosis, 4th paragraph (stabilised before discharge); the 51.6 is from study card sc_srisurapanont_2021. Reworded in all three places, with the source of each statement.

disagreements.first_pass: Ongoing use: in the placebo-controlled trials, craving fell more on aripiprazole and on paliperidone (d = 0.951) than on placebo; the only trial with an objective measure found no difference in methamphetamine-positive urine between aripiprazole and placebo at the end (52.6% to 42.9% vs 55.6% to 43.8%).
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 21: corrected: d = 0.951 is the within-arm fall in craving on paliperidone (the placebo arm's within-arm d is 0.761), not a between-group effect; the between-group comparison is p = 0.03 (Wang 2019, Table 3 2c), and for aripiprazole p = 0.015 on the BSCS with no effect size (Sulaiman 2013); the review's text presents 0.951 as superiority over placebo. Missed: the printed paliperidone baseline SD of 0.08 is probably 0.8; the printed d values are approached only with SD 0.8 and end-point numbers of 29 and 18.
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed in Table 3, section 2c (Wang 2019: MCS 4 (SD 0.08) to 3.2 (0.9) and 4.4 (1) to 3.7 (0.7), d 0.951 and 0.761, between-group p 0.03; Sulaiman 2013: BSCS between-group 0.015, footnote d) and Ongoing substance use, 1st paragraph. Recomputed by the review's formula: 1.252 as printed, 0.949 with SD 0.8 and n 29, 0.761 for placebo with n 18. Finding rewritten; the calculation added as a note labelled as the editors'.

disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 21: missed: Table 3 2a-1 gives Wang 2016 a between-group p = 0.01 on the Simpson–Angus Scale (aripiprazole 0.1 to 3.4, risperidone 0.2 to 3); Fluyau 2019 reports no significant difference between the drugs on that scale, so the reviews disagree on this trial's side effects.
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed in Table 3, section 2a-1 (Wang 2016 row, between-group 0.01), and in the 2019 review (Side Effects › Aripiprazole, Risperidone: no statistical difference on SAS and BARS). Added as a note to the tolerability finding.

disagreements.first_pass: diagnoses described as methamphetamine psychosis or methamphetamine dependence with psychosis in six trials and as amphetamine psychosis in two (Farnia 2014; Leelahanaj 2005) (Table 1).
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 21: missed: Table 1 gives Sulaiman 2013's diagnosis as amphetamine dependence (DSM-IV/5), with methamphetamine use and psychotic symptoms as the threshold, so five trials, not six, are labelled as methamphetamine psychosis or dependence, and three are labelled by amphetamine.
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed in Table 1, Dx and severity-threshold entries of all eight trials. Corrected.

disagreements.first_pass: The discussion of ongoing use attributes the larger reduction in craving on risperidone than on aripiprazole to Wang et al. (2019), a paliperidone–placebo trial; in Table 3 the comparison is Wang et al. (2016).
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 21: missed (minor): the Ongoing substance use paragraph gives paliperidone 27%–75% of the BNF maximum; Table 1 gives 25%–75%.
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed in Results › Secondary outcomes › Ongoing substance use, 1st paragraph, against Table 1 (Wang 2020 row). Added to the issue on the same paragraph.

disagreements.first_pass: risk_of_bias.domains[3].judgment: partial-yes; risk_of_bias.overall: low-confidence; risk_of_bias.domains[3].note: Not met for 'yes': no consultation of content experts is reported, and the restriction to peer-reviewed literature is neither justified nor kept (a dissertation is included).
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 21: agree with every item and with low confidence on the lenient reading; but AMSTAR 2's partial yes on item 4 needs any publication restriction to be justified, and the review restricts eligibility to peer-reviewed literature without a reason (and then includes a dissertation), so the logic of senior decision 21 ('an unjustified language limit is no') would make item 4 'no' here too, which adds a second critical flaw and makes the overall critically low.
disagreements.resolution: Applied AMSTAR 2 item 4 as written, as the adjudication brief directs (and as batch 3 did for the published-only limit in sc_voce_2019): Methods › Eligibility criteria › Study design/characteristics restricts the review to peer-reviewed literature, and neither the Methods nor the Discussion gives a reason, so partial yes is not available. With item 7 also not met, two critical items fail and the overall, recomputed from the critical items, is critically low. Both readers judged every other item the same way and both said the strict reading gives no, so no disagreement on the overall remains; the lenient reading, which would restore low confidence, is listed for the senior author.
